54|Abstract: This study aims to investigate the effect of a preoperative telerehabilitation (PT) program
55|on muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), and functional outcomes in candidates for total
56|knee arthroplasty (TKA). Sixty patients (all women, mean age 70.53 ± 2.7 years) scheduled for
57|bilateral TKA participated in this study. The PT and preoperative patient education (PE) groups
58|participated in a 3-week intensive exercise program (30 min/session, 2 times/day, 5 days/week),
59|whereas the control group received the usual care before TKA. Quadriceps muscle strength, Western
60|Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC), ROM of knee flexion, pain, and
61|time up-and-go (TUG) test time were evaluated at 4 weeks preoperatively, post-interventionally,
62|and 6 weeks after TKA. Significant differences were found in the time-by-group interaction for
63|60◦/s extension peak torque [F(4, 100) = 2.499, p = 0.047, η2p = 0.91], 180◦/s extension peak torque
64|[F(4, 100) = 3.583, p = 0.009, η2p = 0.125], ROM [F(4, 100) = 4.689, p = 0.002, η2p = 0.158], TUG time
65|[F(4, 100) = 7.252, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.225], WOMAC pain [F(4, 100) = 9.113, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.267],
66|WOMAC functional outcome [F(4, 100) = 6.579, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.208], and WOMAC total score
67|[F(4, 100) = 10.410, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.294]. The results of this study demonstrate the early benefits of
68|a PT program in elderly female patients with end-stage osteoarthritis. The PT program improved
69|muscle strength, ROM, and functional outcomes before TKA, which contributed to better functional
70|recovery after TKA.
71|Keywords: osteoarthritis; prehabilitation; telerehabilitation; total knee arthroplasty
72|1. Introduction
73|Osteoarthritis is a common chronic disease in elderly people aged >65 years, and
74|patients with knee osteoarthritis experience pain, swelling, limited joint mobility, and
75|stiffness due to inflammation of the synovial joint [1-3]. To improve the pain and physical
76|function of patients with knee osteoarthritis, previous studies have proposed effective
77|physical therapy interventions, such as manual therapy, physical agent treatment, use
78|of brace and orthoses, aerobic walking, strengthening training, balance training, home-
79|based exercises, self-management programs, and weight reduction programs [4]. However,
80|although these physical therapy interventions have demonstrated valuable results, patients
81|with end-stage knee osteoarthritis still consider undergoing total knee arthroplasty (TKA)
82|to improve their physical performance and quality of life [5].
83|TKA is a surgical procedure that replaces a damaged knee with an artificial prosthesis.
84|It has been suggested as an effective solution for decreasing pain and for the recovery
85|of physical function in patients with end-stage knee osteoarthritis, owing to advances
86|Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2021, 18, 6071. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18116071
87|https://www.mdpi.com/journal/ijerph

1|Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2021, 18, 6071
2|2 of 15
3|in artificial prosthesis design and surgical technology over the past decades [6,7]. By
4|2030, the number of primary TKA procedures performed is expected to increase by 673%
5|to 3.48 million cases in the United States [8]. Meanwhile, primary TKA is performed
6|in >75,000 cases annually in Korea (Statistics Korea). Despite reports about relevant
7|outcomes in terms of pain, functional recovery, and quality of life after a successful TKA,
8|patients still complain of persistent impairments in physical function, muscle strength, and
9|balance ability until the first year after surgery [9,10]. Prior studies have demonstrated
10|a wide range of physical therapy interventions that aim to achieve efficient physical and
11|functional outcomes after TKA [11]. Preoperative muscle strength and physical function
12|may contribute to postoperative outcomes; however, most physical therapy interventions
13|for TKA rehabilitation are focused on the postoperative period [12,13].
14|The concept of prehabilitation (or preoperative rehabilitation), including medical or
15|behavioral support interventions such as exercise, physical therapy, and lifestyle modi-
16|fications performed before surgery, has been implemented in patients with cancer, car-
17|diopulmonary diseases, and musculoskeletal diseases, with reported beneficial effects [14].
18|Recent studies have found that a preoperative rehabilitation program for patients sched-
19|uled to undergo TKA improves postoperative pain, range of motion (ROM), balance ability,
20|stiffness, muscle strength, length of hospital stay (LOS), and health-related quality of life;
21|however, the effectiveness of preoperative interventions varied with intervention protocols
22|such as intensity, frequency, the content of the program, and duration of intervention, and
23|is still controversial [15-19].
24|The implementation of telerehabilitation in physical therapy can enable the remote
25|delivery of personalized assessment and treatment intervention through the use of digital
26|technology, thereby providing the advantages of treatment accessibility and cost reduc-
27|tion for patients living in areas far from rehabilitation facilities [20,21]. The application
28|of telerehabilitation has increased along with technological developments, and previous
29|studies have shown the potential of telerehabilitation as an alternative to hospital-based
30|rehabilitation. In fact, a study on home-based physical therapy through telephone calls
31|demonstrated beneficial effects on pain and physical function in patients with knee os-
32|teoarthritis [22]. In addition, telerehabilitation in patients undergoing TKA has been shown
33|to have similar treatment effects to face-to-face treatment in terms of pain relief, ROM of
34|the knee, quadriceps strength, and physical function [23]. Furthermore, a preoperative
35|telerehabilitation program for patients who are candidates for TKA has been shown to
36|provide benefits in terms of early-phase outcomes after TKA; however, the recent study of
37|preoperative-telerehabilitation has reported no effect on muscle strength and functional
38|outcomes and the efficacy of tele-prehabilitation is lacking evidence from multiple per-
39|spectives [24,25]. Moreover, there were no preoperative telerehabilitation programs that
40|combined intensive training for candidates who are waiting only for a short period for
41|TKA in various medical systems. The purpose of this study is to investigate the effects of
42|a preoperative telerehabilitation program with intensive training for 3 weeks on muscle
43|strength, ROM, and functional outcomes in patients undergoing TKA.
44|2. Materials and Methods
45|2.1. Participants
46|Patients who were scheduled to undergo primary TKA for the treatment of advanced
47|knee osteoarthritis were recruited from an orthopedic surgery rehabilitation hospital. The
48|inclusion criteria for participation in this preoperative telerehabilitation program were as
49|follows: (1) scheduled bilateral TKA, (2) age ranging from 65 to 75 years, (3) efficient control
50|of comorbid diseases, (4) ability to walk over 10 m without help, (5) average vision and
51|hearing, (6) consent to voluntary participation in the preoperative rehabilitation program
52|with prior consent from the surgeon, (7) without cognitive impairment and with good com-
53|munication ability, and (8) familiarity with smartphone apps. The exclusion criteria were
54|as follows: (1) medical instability such as uncontrolled hypertension and arrhythmia or an
55|unstable cardiovascular status, (2) inflammatory arthritis, (3) scheduled TKA revision, (4)

1|Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2021, 18, 6071
2|3 of 15
3|history of knee surgery within 6 months, (5) neurological disorders (including Parkinson's
4|disease and stroke), and (6) neurological damage to the lower extremity.
5|2.2. Ethical Statement
6|Before participation in this study, the test and intervention protocols were fully ex-
7|plained to, and written informed consent was obtained from the patients or their caregivers.
8|This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was ap-
9|proved by the institutional review board of Sahmyook University in the Republic of Korea
10|(2-7001793-AB-N-012019032HR). The protocol of this trial was retrospectively registered
11|with the Clinical Research Information Service of the Republic of Korea (KCT0005800).
12|2.3. Study Design
13|The present study was a three-arm, parallel-group, single-blind randomized controlled
14|trial. A total of 231 patients who were scheduled to undergo TKA were assessed for
15|eligibility. Of them, 171 patients were excluded. For sample size determination in this study,
16|we performed a power analysis using G*Power (version 3.1.9.4; Heinrich-Heine-Universität,
17|Düsseldorf, Germany, 2019) before participant recruitment. The overall effect size index
18|for all outcome measures and the power of the study were both 0.25; the probability was
19|0.05; type II error (power 95%) was minimized; the number of groups was 3; and the
20|number of measurements was 3. As the estimated target sample size was 54, we recruited
21|60 participants who were scheduled for TKA [26]; the random allocation was generated by
22|a research nurse not involved in this study using a computerized random number generator.
23|After the baseline assessment, 60 patients who consented to participate and were eligible
24|for randomization were allocated to the experimental 1 (preoperative telerehabilitation)
25|group, experimental 2 (patient education) group, or control group by each patient choosing
26|one of three envelopes. The group assignments were concealed in envelopes. The assessors
27|and participants were blinded to the group assignments. The assessors who measured all
28|baseline data, post-intervention data, and postoperative outcomes were unaware of the
29|participants' allocation, and all measurements were performed in an independent room.
30|All interventions were individually performed. The enrollment period was from August
31|2019 to April 2020.
32|2.4. Procedure
33|The preoperative telerehabilitation intervention was conducted 3 weeks before the
34|TKA procedure. Therefore, examinations were performed at three time points. Baseline
35|data and post-intervention data were collected at 4 weeks and 1 day before the TKA
36|procedure, respectively. Follow-up was completed at 6 weeks after TKA. These three
37|measurement points were used to evaluate the effect of the preoperative intervention on
38|the patients' physical function, pain, muscle strength, activities of daily living, and quality
39|of life after TKA.
40|After the completion of the experimental procedure, all participants underwent TKA
41|with the same type of high-flexion mobile prosthesis (Implantcast; GMBH Lüneburger
42|Schanze, Buxtehude, Germany) with cement using a tricompartmental, minimally invasive
43|quadriceps-sparing technique [27].
44|After TKA, all patients participated in a standardized rehabilitation program for
45|inpatients at an orthopedic rehabilitation hospital for 3 weeks. The postoperative physical
46|therapy program started on the day immediately post-TKA, was performed daily and
47|included continuous passive motion exercises, intermittent pneumatic compression, and
48|cold pack therapy. On the second postoperative day, weight-bearing with the aid of a
49|walker was started after drain removal and wearing a compression stocking, cryotherapy,
50|and manual therapy added for physical therapy. For the first and second weeks, the
51|patients completed knee ROM exercises, ankle pumping, straight leg raises, self-passive
52|knee extension, balance training, and gait training with a walker. In the third week, strength
53|training, endurance exercise, and walking up and down stairs were added (Figure 1).

5|2.5. Interventions
6|2.5.1. Preoperative Telerehabilitation Group
7|The intervention group participated in a preoperative telerehabilitation program
8|(30 min/session, 2 times/day, 5 days/week for 3 weeks, for a total of 30 sessions) be-
9|fore TKA. The protocol of the preoperative telerehabilitation program is described in
10|Appendix A. Each session included warm-up, mobility, flexibility, strength, balance, and
11|cool-down exercises. The warm-up and cool-down exercises consisted of knee and ankle
12|ROM exercises and slow walking for 5 min. During the mobility exercises, the patients
13|completed straight leg raises, bridges, leg slides, knee press, passive ROM, and mini squats.
14|After the mobility exercises, the patients performed flexibility exercises consisting of knee
15|extensor stretching, knee flexor stretching, and leg slides. For strengthening exercises that
16|involved knee flexor, knee extensor, and hip abductor training, we used elastic resistance
17|bands such as Thera-Band® (Hygienic Corporation, Akron, OH, USA). The intensity of
18|the resistance was adjusted to a moderate level for each patient. After the strengthening
19|exercises, the patients performed balance exercises that included tandem walk and trunk
20|rotation. These exercises were designed to have medium to low intensity that would not
21|cause pain in the knees of patients with end-stage osteoarthritis. The total exercise time
22|was set to 30 min, and the rest time was set to 20 s. Additional rest time was allowed when
23|fatigue occurred or on a patient's request. All interventions were performed at home using
24|a smartphone or tablet via a two-way video call. The therapist provided supervision and
25|intervention with real-time visual feedback and verbal cues. The patients participated in a

1|Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2021, 18, 6071
2|5 of 15
3|comfortable position using an assistive device that can distribute weight while standing
4|or sitting.
5|2.5.2. Preoperative Patient Education Group
6|The preoperative patient education group initially participated in a preoperative
7|education session, which consisted of home exercise safety and the protocol of intervention
8|details for 40 min and thereafter performed a self-home exercise. This non-supervised
9|intervention was performed for 30 min per session, 2 times/day, 5 days/week for 3 weeks,
10|and the exercise timing was adjustable. A physical therapist checked physical condition
11|and provided daily notification, motivation and education of the preoperative exercise via
12|telephone calls once every day. The intervention protocol was the same as the preoperative
13|telerehabilitation program and the patients were encouraged to complete each exercise.
14|The intensity of each exercise was designed to not exacerbate the pain. The exercise details
15|were described in the patient guidebook.
16|2.5.3. Control Group
17|The control group received the usual care, such as following the guideline of surgical
18|procedure, postoperative progress monitoring, discharge destination determination, and
19|simple quadriceps exercise intervention. The exercise was recommended to be performed
20|several times daily as the patient's condition determined.
21|2.6. Primary Outcome Measures
22|Isokinetic Strength Assessment
23|Quadriceps strength was measured using a dynamometer (Biodex 3 PRO; Biodex
24|Medical Systems Inc., Shirley, NY, USA, 2015). The test-retest reliability showed a high
25|intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.947-0.966 in patients who underwent TKA [28].
26|During the measurement, the patient's chest, abdomen, thigh, and ankles were fixed with
27|a strap, and the dynamometer rotation axis was aligned with the knee joint axis. Isokinetic
28|force was measured with knee flexion at 60◦/s and 180◦/s peak torque (N-m) and knee
29|extension at 60/sec◦and 180◦/s peak torque (N-m) [29]. The average value of all three
30|trials was used for statistical analysis.
31|2.7. Secondary Outcome Measures
32|2.7.1. Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC)
33|The WOMAC [ICC = 0.96, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.94-0.98] evaluates the pain,
34|stiffness, and function of patients with knee osteoarthritis who have undergone TKA [30].
35|This tool has a total of 24 items, consisting of 5 pain items, 2 stiffness items, and 17 functional
36|items. It is a five-point scale from 0 (lowest) to 4 (highest) for each item, with a lower score
37|indicating fewer symptoms and less physical disability [31].
38|2.7.2. Knee Flexion ROM
39|The self-passive knee flexion ROM was measured using a digital goniometer (Biomet-
40|rics, Baton Rouge, LA, USA, 2008), which showed good intrarater ICC of 0.997-0.998 and
41|interrater reliability ICC of 0.994 for knee joint ROM [32]. To measure the knee ROM, the
42|axis of the digital goniometer was attached to the lateral joint space of the knee; the fixed
43|arm was placed in the middle of the femur, between the greater trochanter and the lateral
44|joint space of the knee; and the moving arm was lined up with the lateral malleolus of the
45|fibula [33]. After the measurement, the angle of goniometer was reset to zero and the trial
46|was repeated three times.
47|2.7.3. Timed Up-and-Go (TUG) Test
48|The TUG test (ICC = 0.54-0.97) is used to assess dynamic balance ability and to
49|predict falls in the elderly population [34]. In this study, the participants stood up from an
50|armless chair upon the assessor's signal, walked to the 3-m point, and returned to sit on

1|Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2021, 18, 6071
2|6 of 15
3|the same chair. The test was performed three times, and the average value of the TUG time
4|was obtained.
5|2.7.4. Pressure Pain Threshold
6|The pressure pain threshold (kg/cm2) was measured using a digital pressure algome-
7|ter (Pain TestTMFPX 25 Algometer; Wagner Instrument, Greenwich, CT, USA, 2015) at the
8|vastus medialis; a position four fingers above the medial epicondyle. The measurement
9|was performed while avoiding the surgical site (Cronbach's alpha = 0.94-0.98) [35]. The
10|average value of three trials was used in the analysis.
11|2.8. Data Analysis
12|The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was used to ensure the normal distribution of the data

23|group, and control (usual care) group. The flow of patients throughout the study is shown
24|in Figure 1. All participants were women aged >65 years with Kellgren-Lawrence grade
25|3-4 osteoarthritis that underwent TKA. The patient demographics are shown in Table 1.

113|4. Discussion
114|This study aimed to investigate the effect of a preoperative telerehabilitation program
115|on muscle strength, ROM, and functional outcomes in patients undergoing TKA. The
116|findings of this study indicated that the preoperative telerehabilitation program had a
117|positive effect on the outcomes after TKA. It improved the patient-reported functional out-
118|comes, muscle strength, and ROM of patients with end-stage osteoarthritis who underwent
119|TKA. The patients reported better pain scores at 6 weeks after TKA. In contrast, no close
120|relationship was found between patient-reported pain and pressure pain threshold at the
121|three time points.
122|A.
123|Isokinetic Muscle Strength
124|Reduced quadriceps strength is commonly observed in patients immediately after
125|TKA, and it takes from 6 months to 1 year to regain the preoperative values [36]. Weakness
126|of the quadriceps affects neuromuscular activation and functional ability, leading to an
127|increased risk of falls in patients undergoing TKA [37]. High-intensive preoperative
128|training that included resistance training exercise and strengthening exercise for 3 days per
129|week for 8 weeks improved isometric knee extension value after training and 3 months
130|after TKA compared with the control group [26]. Similarly, Swank et al. reported on the

1|Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2021, 18, 6071
2|10 of 15
3|prehabilitation program that included resistance training with elastic bands, flexibility,
4|and step training 3 times per week for 4-8 weeks significantly improved knee extension
5|peak torque in the surgical leg after the intervention [38]. In this study, the intervention
6|protocol included training of knee extensors and resistance exercise with Thera-Band. It
7|may impact increasing knee extension peak torque after intervention and 6 weeks after
8|TKA. The extension strength of the PT group and PE group increased after intervention
9|and had decreased less after 6 weeks TKA compared to the control group. Compared to the
10|mean value of 60◦/s extension peak torque between groups, the PT group and PE showed
11|a decrease of 11.5% and 11.37%, respectively, whereas the control group showed 40.13%
12|at baseline to post-TKA. In 180◦/s extension peak torque, the TP and PE groups showed
13|a decrease of 6.17% and 22.98%, respectively, whereas the control group showed 31.9%
14|at baseline to post-TKA. Although the PT group spent more time exercising than the PE
15|group, this result was probably due to the protocol of the prehabilitation program being the
16|same and the motivation and education successfully provided in both groups by physical
17|therapists. The less decreased extension strength was a significant predictor for recovery of
18|postoperative muscle strength and the possibility of easy regain of preoperative values. We
19|did not consider minimal clinical important difference (MCID) in muscle strength because
20|there was no evidence in our candidates for TKA [39].
21|B.
22|Functional outcomes
23|A patient with end-stage knee osteoarthritis experiences severe pain when in a weight
24|bearing position and experiences physical function difficulties when performing every-
25|day activities along with weakness of leg strength [40]. Pain and limitation of physical
26|function in osteoarthritis patients eventually decrease the patient's quality of life, which
27|is a major reason for patients to consider TKA. After successful TKA, a decrease in pain
28|and improvement of physical function promotes functional activities and ADL such as
29|walking, climbing, sit-to-stand movement, self-care, and housekeeping. The preoperative
30|knee ROM, pain, and functional ability predict postoperative outcomes among patients
31|undergoing TKA [41]. The present study conducted tele-prehabilitation that consists of
32|mobility, flexibility, strengthening exercise (using elastic band) and balance exercise for
33|3 weeks before TKA and found improvements in all outcomes such as knee ROM, WOMAC
34|points, and TUG time. The knee flexion ROM was measured self-passively using a dig-
35|ital goniometer. This increased from 107◦to 114◦at pre-post intervention and 138◦at
36|6 weeks after TKA in the PT group, from 108◦to 110◦at pre-post intervention and 131◦
37|at 6 weeks after TKA in the PE group. The control group increased from 110◦to 107◦at
38|pre-post intervention and was measured as 127◦at 6 weeks after TKA. The PT group and
39|PE group had been trained in knee ROM exercise and quadriceps stretching and these may
40|be influenced by the increasing knee ROM in comparison to the control group. Regarding
41|the WOMAC score, a significant difference was reported in the time-by-group interaction
42|of all subscales and total score. The minimal clinical important improvement (MCII) for
43|WOMAC recommended a 12% improvement from baseline for OA [42]. The baseline value
44|of the PT group was 65.89 and improved 9.83 points at pre-post intervention over more
45|than 7.9 (12%). Although the self-reported WOMAC pain score differed significantly, the
46|PPT showed no effect. In TUG time, the minimal detectable change (MDC) is recommended
47|as 1.14 s for OA [43] and 2.27 s for TKA [44]. The TUG time in the PT group showed a
48|meaningful decrease of 3.23 s compared to the PE group of 1.12 s and the control group
49|of -0.33 s at pre-post intervention. The TUG time decreased by 4.03 s in the PT group,
50|2.83 s in the PE and 1.36 s in the control group at baseline to 6 weeks post-TKA. The
51|mini squat may promote sit-to-stand movement and help practice timed up-and-go tests.
52|The fall incidents reported one case (5%) in the control group. Therefore, the protocol of
53|this preoperative telerehabilitation program may have positive effects on the ability of
54|patients' balance in the early stages after TKA. Similar to the results of this study, Vasta
55|et al. reported in their systematic review that preoperative physical activity or prehabili-
56|tation (including muscle strengthening with or without elastic resistance, proprioceptive
57|exercise, progressive resistance training, and home-based exercise program) at 6 and 3

1|Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2021, 18, 6071
2|11 of 15
3|weeks before TKA in elderly patients improved the pain score, ROM, and functional index
4|compared with the control group [13]. The study by Chughtai et al. (n = 114) demonstrated
5|that patients in the prehabilitation with telerehabilitation group had shorter LOS than the
6|control group [24]. LOS was not measured in the current study because all countries have
7|different healthcare systems, and patients after bilateral TKA typically stay in the hospital
8|for 3 weeks. In a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Chen et al. reported that
9|the prehabilitation group had better outcomes in knee ROM, LOS, and sit-to-stand test
10|than the control group [18]. Despite the benefits of preoperative intervention, some studies
11|have reported no significant difference in quadriceps strength and physical function. In
12|the study by Beaupre et al., 66 patients underwent 6 weeks of preoperative exercise and
13|education before TKA. The study found no difference in knee ROM, WOMAC, and strength
14|between the two groups [15]. Devasenapathy et al. also found that preoperative muscle
15|strength and function had a poor agreement with the outcomes after TKA, and the effect of
16|preoperative intervention lasted for only 6 months to 1 year. Intervention protocols, such as
17|intervention intensity, frequency, duration, and follow-up duration, may contribute to the
18|outcomes. The duration of the intervention varied from 2 to 12 weeks, and the frequency
19|was mainly 2-3 times a week [12]. In this study, we provided 30 sessions for 3 weeks as
20|intensive training for elderly patients. The approaching date of surgery provided sufficient
21|motivation to induce the patient's commitment to treatment, however, two participants
22|discontinued their participation due to the high intensity. We did not verify the long-term
23|effects of preoperative telerehabilitation but observed improvements in physical function
24|and restoration of muscle strength in the early phase after TKA.
25|This study had several limitations. First, the sample size was small and only female
26|participants were included. Although the results of the present study showed improve-
27|ments in muscle strength and functional outcomes, a large sample size is required to
28|provide definitive evidence on the effect of preoperative telerehabilitation. Moreover, our
29|sample consisting of female patients does not represent the typical cases. In addition, this
30|study provides only data on the short-term outcomes (at 6 weeks after TKA) of preoperative
31|telerehabilitation, and we could not control for the use of pain medications in the early
32|phase after TKA. Therefore, long-term follow-up is required to prove the independent
33|effects on pain, excluding the bias of this program. This study attempted to maximize the
34|treatment effect by applying real-time telerehabilitation, and there was a limitation in the
35|composition of the protocol as a non-face-to-face intervention that prioritized the safety
36|of elderly patients with end-stage osteoarthritis. Further studies with a large sample size
37|and including typical participants are needed. Furthermore, long-term follow-up data are
38|required before the broad application of this preoperative telerehabilitation program.
39|5. Conclusions
40|The present study demonstrates the early benefits of a preoperative telerehabilitation
41|program in elderly female patients with end-stage osteoarthritis. This preoperative telere-
42|habilitation program improved muscle strength, ROM, and functional outcomes in patients
43|before TKA, which contributed to better functional recovery after TKA.
